title: Conditional Collapse in Sign Language Production:A Diagnostic and a Scaling Argument

paper.title: Conditional Collapse in Sign Language Production: A Diagnostic and a Scaling Argument
paper.abstract:
Abstract Sign Language Production (SLP) is the task of generating avatar sign
language motion from natural language text. The quality of the
generated motion is typically evaluated by a motion-space Fréchet
distance (FID) and back-translation (BT) BLEU score on benchmarks
such as How2Sign. Both metrics can improve substantially while the
underlying generator fails to faithfully represent the sign language
gestures. In this work we propose to evaluate the generated motion
at three independent levels: ( τ 1 \tau_{1} ) initial-pose conditioning,
( τ 2 \tau_{2} ) output diversity, and ( τ 3 \tau_{3} ) target faithfulness. We
compute these as pairwise-distance ratios using latent representations
of a frozen motion autoencoder (MoAE). We evaluate 14 14 SLP model
checkpoints on How2Sign dataset ( Duarte et al., 2021 ) , including a re-implemented Neural Sign
Actors (NSA) ( Baltatzis et al., 2024 ) , and show that τ 3 \tau_{3} faithfulness is never attained, while FID varies by nearly two orders
of magnitude and is uncorrelated with faithfulness. We show that on the isolated gloss
dataset ASL3DWord ( Dong et al., 2024a ) favorable τ 3 \tau_{3} can be attained,
hence isolating the size of the sentence-level paired-dataset as the bottleneck.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Text-to-motion systems report steady improvements on standard quantitative benchmarks. Reliable evaluation of text-to-motion generation requires metrics that respond to whether each output is faithful to its specific input, not merely to whether outputs look like plausible samples from the training distribution. We study this requirement in sentence-level Sign Language Production (SLP), where recent systems on How2Sign ( Duarte et al., 2021 ) report steadily improving Fréchet distance (FID), computed over motion features, and back-translation (BT) BLEU score, and declare progress toward usable text-to-sign generation. We argue that both headline metrics can rise while the underlying generator remains essentially text-independent. FID rewards an anatomically valid mean motion that ignores the input over a model that follows the input but produces slightly noisier motion. It can thus prefer a collapsed generator over a faithful one, as we observe on How2Sign (§ 5.2 ); back-translation BLEU is bounded by a BT model that itself collapses to high-frequency boilerplate, so it reflects token-frequency overlap rather than motion-text correspondence. In this work, we propose novel evaluation and diagnostic metrics that reveal conditional collapse in Sign Language Production on state-of-the-art datasets.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: (i) Given any text-to-motion model and a held-out test set, we encode both ground-truth motions and model generations through a frozen motion autoencoder MoAE (a small transformer) trained once on the target dataset’s ground-truth motions, compressing each motion into a compact latent vector and reconstructing it. We then compute three pairwise-distance ratios in that space, varying the sentence conditioning and comparing the generated and ground-truth motions. (ii) We identify three indicators of conditional collapse at different levels: an initial-pose level ( τ 1 \tau_{1} ), an output diversity level ( τ 2 \tau_{2} ), and a faithfulness level ( τ 3 \tau_{3} ) that can be attained independently , with visual and quantitative evidence (§ 4 ). (iii) We transfer the same generative diffusion model backbone to the gloss-level ASL3DWord benchmark, showing that it attains significantly better τ 3 \tau_{3} , suggesting that sentence-level paired-data scale is a major bottleneck for How2Sign within the architecture space we tested (§ 5.4 , Figure 3 ). The failures we document are diagnosable and motivate three concrete changes. The field should (a) report the diagnostic ratios alongside FID and back-translation BLEU; (b) be transparent about the paired-data budget and any auxiliary pretraining corpora; and (c) treat the faithfulness level ( τ 3 \tau_{3} ) as an important criterion when designing future models (§ 6 ).

sections.heading: Sign Language Production.
sections.text: Sentence-level SLP approaches fall into two families. Regression-based approaches formulate the problem as sequence to (continuous) pose sequence translation and predict a deterministic pose stream: Progressive Transformers (PT) ( Saunders et al., 2020 ) use an autoregressive transformer with a learned step-counter scalar over a T5-style text encoder; Huang et al. (2021) replace the autoregressive decoder with a non-autoregressive parallel decoder, an external aligner for gloss-duration prediction, and a spatial-temporal graph-convolutional pose generator on Phoenix-2014T; T2S-GPT ( Yin et al., 2024 ) encodes Phoenix-2014T SMPL-X poses with a dynamic-length VQ-VAE and autoregressively generates pose codes from text with a GPT-style decoder. Diffusion-based approaches train a generative model of human motion conditioned on text describing human action sequences. For example MDM ( Tevet et al., 2023 ) is a transformer denoising model conditioned on text describing general sequences of actions encoded with a frozen CLIP encoder; G2P-DDM ( Xie et al., 2024 ) encodes Phoenix-2014T poses with a VQ-VAE and runs discrete denoising diffusion in the discrete latent space; Neural Sign Actors ( Baltatzis et al., 2024 ) uses a GNN + LSTM denoising model on SMPL-X parameters. Hong and Kosecka (2026) build a MDM-style backbone at the gloss level on ASL3DWord ( Dong et al., 2024a ) (a WLASL ( Li et al., 2020 ) subset; 1.2 1.2 K clips, 103 103 glosses) and report usable generation; we apply the same backbone to sentence-level How2Sign and find that gloss-scale conclusions do not transfer. Sign Language Translation (SLT) SLP approaches are often evaluated by back-translating generated human motions to text using a learned sign-to-text model, and reporting BLEU score. Three SLT families recur: the joint CSLR + + SLT Sign Language Transformers ( Camgoz et al., 2020 ) , which couples a gloss-CTC loss with translation; plain encoder–decoders over pretrained video features (e.g. Tarrés et al. (2023) , Kinetics-I3D, no gloss-CTC); and discrete-token translation pretrained on large corpora (YouTube-ASL ( Uthus et al., 2023 ) , 11 11 K hours). The two recurring datasets differ in vocabulary, reporting low BLEU-4 score for non-pretrained BT models: weather-domain Phoenix-2014T ( Forster et al., 2014 ) has ∼ \sim 1,066 1{,}066 German (DGS) gloss types in ∼ \sim 7 7 K sentence-motion pairs, whereas on open-domain How2Sign ( Duarte et al., 2021 ) ( ∼ \sim 15 15 K words, ∼ \sim 31 31 K pairs) the highest attained BLEU-4 score is far lower. In the no-pretraining regime Uthus et al. (2023) report How2Sign BLEU-4 ≈ 1.22 \approx 1.22 and our own BT model plateaus at a BLEU-4 ceiling of ≈ 2.5 \approx 2.5 even on GT motion; Tarrés et al. (2023) reach 8.03 8.03 via I3D pretraining and Uthus et al. (2023) ≈ 12 \approx 12 via pre-training on 11 11 K hours of videos from YouTubeASL dataset. By contrast, Saunders et al. (2020) and Baltatzis et al. (2024) report BLEU-4 of 10.51 10.51 and 13.12 13.12 without describing auxiliary pretraining, the latter exceeding both the pretrained YouTube-ASL number and our GT-motion BLEU-4 score. Independent re-trainings of Progressive Transformers (PT) in the three SLP papers above place BLEU-4 well below these numbers. Huang et al. (2021) retrain PT on OpenPose 3D joints (gloss-to-pose, no GT timing at inference) and report BLEU-4 1.59 1.59 for the base model and 4.04 4.04 for the future-prediction/Gaussian-noise variant. Xie et al. (2024) report 4.04 4.04 BLEU-4 and note that PT’s original numbers depend on ground-truth first-frame and timing information. Yin et al. (2024) retrain PT on a SMPL-X 6 6 D-rotation representation (text-to-pose) and report BLEU-4 of 4.38 4.38 . Across two input representations and both task settings, independently retrained PTs fall in the 1.6 1.6 – 4.4 4.4 range. FID critiques. The limitations of Frechet Distance (FID) for conditional generation are well known in the text-to-image ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2023 ) and text-to-motion ( Guo et al., 2022 ) literatures, and alternatives such as paired R-precision, MM-Distance and MultiModality have been proposed. Our diagnostic is in this spirit but specifically targets the conditional-mean collapse blindness dominant in SLP. Pose-based SL generation evaluation. Most directly adjacent, Jiang et al. (2025) meta-evaluate existing pose-based sign language metrics by correlation with human judgements and rank them by quality. We instead diagnose why the generators themselves fail, decomposing conditional collapse into three levels and attributing it to paired-data scale.

sections.heading: 3.1 Stability of the diagnostic
sections.text: We compute these diagnostics for a large variety of models and restrictions on train and test datasets. The numbers in Table 1 use the full test split of each dataset, so the reported values do not depend on which subsample of test sentences is drawn. Even on the full test split, almost every SLP model we test gives ρ faith ≈ 1 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}\approx 1 . A fair concern is that this value reflects a problem with the metric itself, not with the models: either (i) the MoAE cannot tell motions apart in its latent space, or (ii) ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} always returns ≈ 1 \approx 1 regardless of input. We rule both out with two checks. (1) MoAE initialization. Re-training the MoAE from a different random initialization (same architecture and data) and re-running the diagnostic preserves the relative ordering of all measured main-table checkpoints; the diagnostic is robust to MoAE training noise and not an artefact of one particular MoAE fit. (2) GT-vs-GT check: can ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} ever move? To rule out (ii), we feed the diagnostic the strongest possible “alignment” case: use the GT motion itself in place of the model output. sections.heading: 4 Three Diagnostic Levels of Conditional Collapse
sections.text: The diagnostic ratios decompose SLP failure into three independent levels , denoted τ 1 \tau_{1} , τ 2 \tau_{2} , τ 3 \tau_{3} : τ 1 \tau_{1} : Initial-pose level. Satisfied when the model’s t = 0 t=0 pose varies as a function of the input text ( varied ); failed when every generated initial pose is identical across sentences ( frozen ). Visually inspectable in rendered output. τ 2 \tau_{2} : Output diversity level. Satisfied when outputs vary across different inputs as much as GT motions do across sentences ( ρ div ∈ [ 0.5 , 2.0 ] \rho_{\mathrm{div}}\in[0.5,2.0] ); failed when outputs cluster around a near-identical mean motion ( ρ div → 0 \rho_{\mathrm{div}}\to 0 ). τ 3 \tau_{3} : Faithfulness level. Satisfied when each output aligns to its specific target GT and not to a random one ( ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} near the dataset’s GT-vs-GT value); failed when alignment is no better than random ( ρ faith ≈ 1 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}\approx 1 ; Section 3 ). The central empirical finding of this paper is that these three diagnostic levels are independently attainable : a model can satisfy τ 1 \tau_{1} and τ 2 \tau_{2} without attaining τ 3 \tau_{3} , but on How2Sign, no configuration we tested attains satisfactory τ 3 \tau_{3} . Every checkpoint we evaluated falls into one of three cases: (i) Frozen start + jitter trajectory ( τ 1 \tau_{1} , τ 2 \tau_{2} , τ 3 \tau_{3} all collapsed). The dominant How2Sign 26K failure mode is a near-identical canonical start regardless of input, then small-amplitude noise around the GT marginal mean. Covers essentially all full-corpus sentence-level checkpoints, including our prior ablation’s FID champion. (ii) Varied start + jitter trajectory ( τ 1 \tau_{1} satisfactory, τ 2 \tau_{2} satisfactory, τ 3 \tau_{3} collapsed). A visibly different start per input, but the trajectory is still noise, not coherent signing. Appears only under aggressive input-distribution narrowing: small vocabularies or short sentences (configurations in § 5 and Appendix A ). (iii) Varied start + coherent motion ( τ 1 \tau_{1} , τ 2 \tau_{2} , τ 3 \tau_{3} all satisfactory). This case is never observed on How2Sign and is reached only on the gloss-level ASL3DWord dataset (§ 5.4 ). Note that for the same dataset configurations that achieve satisfactory τ 1 \tau_{1} and τ 2 \tau_{2} , τ 3 \tau_{3} indicates collapse. Table 1 reports which configurations fall into which case. Figure 1 gives direct visual evidence of the (i) vs (ii) contrast: rows 1 1 – 2 2 emit a near-identical canonical start regardless of input ( τ 1 \tau_{1} collapsed), rows 3 3 – 4 4 show visibly different starts ( τ 1 \tau_{1} satisfied). sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: Throughout this paper we use “checkpoint” to mean one fully trained model from one distinct design configuration (architecture, conditioning input, and dataset subset variant), trained independently from scratch and saved at the best epoch.

sections.heading: Datasets.
sections.text: How2Sign ( Duarte et al., 2021 ) is our primary benchmark. It has 31 31 K training sentences and 2,357 2{,}357 test sentences, with per-frame SMPL-X parameters ( Pavlakos et al., 2019 ) ; average sentence length 17.7 17.7 words and training set vocabulary 15,434 15{,}434 words. ASL3DWord ( Dong et al., 2024a ) (§ 5.4 ) is a gloss-level WLASL-101 dataset, with SMPL-X parameters and 1.2 1.2 K train / 339 339 test clips over 103 103 gloss types. The variants below apply only to How2Sign (rows 1–14 of Table 1 ). We vary two independent aspects of the text input across Table 1 : input modality and training subset. ASL3DWord uses a single English word per sample (one isolated sign, § 5.4 ). Input modality ( sent / gloss ). Sentence : the raw English How2Sign sentence, encoded by frozen CLIP-ViT-B/32 ( Radford et al., 2021 ) . LLM gloss : we prompt an open-source LLM to extract pseudo-glosses (short ordered lists of base-form content words) from sentences; the exact prompt, model, and representative outputs for How2Sign are in Appendix B . A similar LLM-based pseudo-gloss extraction has also been used by Guo et al. (2026) in SLT. ASL gloss annotations are unavailable for How2Sign, so this LLM pseudo-gloss serves as the closest available proxy. Training subset. The unfiltered How2Sign release has 31 31 K training sentences. Our default training pool is the ∼ \sim 26 26 K subset obtained by a 3 3 -to- 30 30 word sentence-length filter that removes long-tail outliers; rows 1–5 and rows 8–14 of Table 1 use this 26 26 K pool. As an end-to-end check that the filter is not load-bearing, we also trained an identical MDM+sentence variant on the unfiltered 31 31 K-sentence release (row 6): ρ faith = 0.98 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.98 matches the 26 26 K run exactly, and the other diagnostic ratios fall in the same band. Beyond these two, we evaluate a 13 13 K random subsample of the 26 26 K pool (row 7) and two families of input-narrowing variants: vocabulary-restricted ( K=K ): sentences whose words all fall within the top- K K most-frequent training vocabulary ( K=3000 , K=500 ); and short-sentence : short1 (single-word) or short3 ( ≤ 3 \leq 3 -word) sentences drawn from the full 31 31 K-sentence release (these bypass the 3 3 -to- 30 30 word filter by design). Exact train/test counts are in Appendix A . Row labels in Table 1 combine the two axes (e.g. K=500 gloss ). Each filter is applied to the raw English sentence regardless of encoder input, so corresponding sent and gloss rows use identical training and test sentences and differ only in what the encoder sees (details in Appendix A ).

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: The variants below are a representative set of recurrent SLP design choices, included as evidence that no point in this space attained τ 3 \tau_{3} faithfulness on How2Sign. We use two architecture families. (i) Diffusion. Our reference backbone is MDM ( Tevet et al., 2023 ) (transformer denoiser, frozen CLIP conditioning). The diffusion rows of Table 1 cover backbone × \times conditioning input: MDM or a multi-scale temporal-transformer variant ( MSTrans ; architecture in Appendix A ) × \times sentence or LLM gloss, all trained with ℒ pose + ℒ FK \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pose}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FK}} (per-frame pose MSE and forward-kinematic joint-position MSE; details in Appendix A ); row 5 5 drops ℒ FK \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FK}} and is the FID-best variant. The cross-attention interface, hyperparameters, the phonology-augmented variant, and per-variant hypotheses are in Appendix A . (ii) Clean transformer decoder regression : a single-pass model where a frozen CLIP text encoder feeds a trainable 6 6 -layer transformer decoder; learned motion-frame queries cross-attend to the CLIP embedding. Trained with ℒ pose + ℒ FK \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pose}}+\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FK}} (details in Appendix A ) with ∼ \sim 26 26 M trainable parameters.

sections.heading: Training.
sections.text: Within each model family, the same training settings are used across all data variants: batch size 256 256 , learning rate 2 × 10 − 4 2\times 10^{-4} , and 100 100 epochs for sentence-length variants; batch size 64 64 and 200 200 epochs for short-sentence variants.

sections.heading: Evaluation.
sections.text: For each checkpoint we compute ( ρ cond , ρ div , ρ faith ) (\rho_{\mathrm{cond}},\rho_{\mathrm{div}},\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}) and FID on the full test split. When training was vocabulary-restricted, we evaluate on the matching test subset (the test sentences whose words also pass the filter). We additionally render generated motions as SMPL-X mesh GIFs and visually inspect them for τ 1 \tau_{1} .

sections.heading: 5.2 The FID– ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} disconnect
sections.text: Across rows 1–14 of Table 1 (rows 15 and 16 are excluded from this FID comparison: row 15 is GT motion itself, and row 16 reports FID in a different MoAE latent space trained on ASL3DWord), FID spans 1.91 1.91 to 151 151 ( ∼ \sim 80 × 80\times ) while ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} spans only 0.89 0.89 to 1.00 1.00 , and the Pearson correlation between them is near zero. The best-FID model ( 1.91 1.91 , MDM+sentence) and the best- ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} model ( 0.89 0.89 , short1 regression) are far apart on the other metric. This shows that FID and faithfulness track different things, and selecting a model by FID alone does not select for genuine text-to-motion alignment.

sections.heading: 5.3 BT-BLEU also fails to track faithfulness
sections.text: We trained a back-translation (motion-to-text) model on How2Sign under the same no-pretraining regime as the published baseline of Uthus et al. (2023) (BLEU-4 ≈ 1.22 \approx 1.22 ). At our best checkpoint, BLEU-4 = 1.24 =1.24 . Inspecting individual predictions (Table 2 ) reveals that the model produces input-independent high-frequency template language filled with instructional constructions (“i’m going to take …”, “you can …”), pronoun-heavy phrases, and end-of-sequence degenerate repetition that is unrelated to the GT sentence. A non-zero BLEU score arises from short n-gram overlap with How2Sign’s high-frequency vocabulary, not from recovered text content. The diagnostic counterpart, ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} , captures this failure directly; BT-BLEU does not. sections.text: We apply the exact same MDM backbone, loss, and diagnostic pipeline to a smaller gloss-level benchmark: ASL3DWord ( Dong et al., 2024a ) (WLASL-101 SMPL-X subset, 1.2 1.2 K train / 339 339 test / 103 103 glosses, T = 60 T{=}60 ), where the task is one English gloss → \to one isolated sign, the opposite end of the data-scale and text-to-motion mapping complexity spectrum from continuous How2Sign sentences. Row 16 of Table 1 reports ρ cond = 4.80 \rho_{\mathrm{cond}}=4.80 , ρ div = 1.14 \rho_{\mathrm{div}}=1.14 , ρ faith = 0.73 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.73 on the full test split: all three ratios are healthy and ρ faith = 0.73 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.73 matches the ASL3DWord GT-vs-GT same-gloss reference ρ faith , ref = 0.752 \rho_{\mathrm{faith,ref}}=0.752 (Eq. 9 ). WLASL records each word with multiple signers, and the same word performed by different signers varies substantially in hand shape and the underlying motion itself. So even a perfect generator that copies a real recording of the target word cannot score below this within-word across-signer floor: ρ faith , ref = 0.752 \rho_{\mathrm{faith,ref}}=0.752 (Eq. 9 ; details in Appendix A ). The diffusion ckpt’s 0.73 0.73 lands right at this floor. Figure 3 shows test-set generations alongside GT; Dong et al. (2024b) similarly report successful word-level 3D ASL generation with a comparable diffusion + + CLIP backbone. sections.heading: Why FID misleads in SLP.
sections.text: Beyond the mean-motion mechanism of § 3 , a model whose outputs match the GT distribution but are paired with the wrong inputs also gets a low FID; neither case matches what a reader expects from a small FID number. The blind spot is worse in SLP because GT motion varies in a small range anatomical envelope) and test sets are typically only a few hundred motions.

sections.heading: Reproducibility note on Neural Sign Actors.
sections.text: Neural Sign Actors ( Baltatzis et al., 2024 ) reports the lowest sentence-level How2Sign FID in the literature but releases neither code nor weights. Following the published description, our re-implementation needed several debugging rounds (gradient-norm clipping, loss-formulation fixes) to converge, and even then our best run reaches FID ≈ 151 \approx 151 (an order of magnitude above the reported value), with ρ faith ≈ 1.00 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}\approx 1.00 and no input-specific motion in rendered samples. We do not interpret this discrepancy, and it does not affect our claim: at the How2Sign 26K budget even an NSA-class FID is consistent with τ 1 \tau_{1} / τ 2 \tau_{2} satisfied + + τ 3 \tau_{3} collapsed, the regime our 14 14 How2Sign checkpoints occupy. We read prior FID gains in this line as improvements in τ 1 \tau_{1} and partial τ 2 \tau_{2} , not τ 3 \tau_{3} .

sections.heading: Recommended evaluation protocol.
sections.text: We recommend SLP papers report all three ratios alongside FID: ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} as a bright-line check (treat ρ faith ≥ 0.95 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}\geq 0.95 as failure), and ρ div \rho_{\mathrm{div}} to separate “random anatomical poses” (low ρ div \rho_{\mathrm{div}} ) from “diverse but mis-aligned outputs” (near-GT ρ div \rho_{\mathrm{div}} ). Computing the diagnostic on a shared external motion MoAE (we release ours, Appendix A ) also removes the per-paper-MoAE inconsistency behind FID drift across the literature. The diagnostic is parameter-free and adds negligible cost on top of standard generation.

sections.heading: Bidirectional evidence of the data bottleneck.
sections.text: The bottleneck is independently visible in the sign-to-text direction. Uthus et al. (2023) report that a translator trained directly on How2Sign reaches only BLEU-4 ≈ 1.22 \approx 1.22 , consistent with output dominated by high-frequency boilerplate (§ 5.3 , Table 2 ), with faithful translation emerging only after 11 11 K hours of pretraining. Our text-to-motion experiments reach the symmetric conclusion: ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} never leaves the collapse band on How2Sign 26K and the 13 13 K → \to 26 26 K gradient does not improve it. The bottleneck is the same in both directions: How2Sign’s 26 26 K paired sentences are below what is needed to learn the motion–text correspondence.

sections.heading: What would satisfy τ 3 \tau_{3} ?
sections.text: The most concrete candidate is large-scale text-to-motion pretraining on an auxiliary corpus: the YouTube-ASL translator becomes faithful in the sign-to-text direction only after 11 11 K hours of pretraining, and a similarly-scaled motion pretrain may transfer to text-to-motion.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced a diagnostic that exposes conditional collapse in sentence-level Sign Language Production, and used it to establish that the How2Sign paired-data scale is a major bottleneck on the faithfulness level ( τ 3 \tau_{3} ) within the architecture space we tested, with collapse persisting across data quantity and input unit length. A best-effort reimplementation of Neural Sign Actors places it in the same τ 3 \tau_{3} -collapsed regime as the rest of our checkpoints, while the same diffusion backbone and loss transferred unchanged to gloss-level ASL3DWord satisfies τ 3 \tau_{3} ( ρ faith = 0.73 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.73 ), consistent with sentence-level paired-data scale being a major bottleneck within the architecture space we tested. The FID–alignment disconnect we document argues for a field-wide protocol change: SLP papers should report ( ρ cond , ρ div , ρ faith ) (\rho_{\mathrm{cond}},\rho_{\mathrm{div}},\rho_{\mathrm{faith}}) alongside FID and BLEU, and treat ρ faith ≥ 0.95 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}\geq 0.95 as a clear failure. We release all our code 1 1 1 https://github.com/hongrui16/slp-diagnostic so that future papers can compute identical ratios.

sections.heading: 8 Limitations
sections.text: Our 14 14 How2Sign checkpoints cover two architecture families and four data axes but do not cover the full design space; in particular, we do not test large-scale text-to-motion pretraining on an auxiliary corpus. The diagnostic has the limitations of any MoAE: a poorly-trained MoAE could in principle push ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} artificially close to 1 1 . We address this with a single frozen MoAE trained on the target dataset’s GT train motions, the MoAE-initialization and GT-vs-GT checks of Section 3.1 , and an independent check against visual classification, which gives the same conclusion on every checkpoint where we did it.

sections.heading: MoAE.
sections.text: The MoAE ϕ \phi used by verify-collapse is a small transformer autoencoder operating on per-frame 3 3 -D joint coordinates: each generated SMPL-X axis-angle sequence is first lifted to T × 144 × 3 T\times 144\times 3 joints by SMPL-X forward kinematics, restricted to the 44 44 upper-body joints (spine, head, shoulders, elbows, wrists, all 30 30 finger joints), and made pelvis-relative, yielding per-frame input dimension D = 132 D=132 . A linear projection lifts each frame to a d model = 256 d_{\mathrm{model}}=256 token; learnable absolute positional embeddings are added; a 3 3 -layer transformer encoder ( 4 4 attention heads, feed-forward dim 512 512 , GELU, pre-LN) produces contextualized per-frame features. A masked mean over valid frames (padding excluded) gives the 256 256 -dim bottleneck z z . The decoder broadcasts z z across the target sequence length, adds the same positional embeddings, runs through another 3 3 -layer transformer stack with the same hyper-parameters, and projects back to D D . Position embeddings are shared between encoder and decoder; padding is handled with a boolean mask in both directions. Training loss. For each batch we minimize per-frame MSE between reconstruction and target plus an α vel = 0.5 \alpha_{\mathrm{vel}}=0.5 MSE on the first-difference (velocity) of the reconstruction: ℒ MoAE = MSE ⁡ ( x ^ , x ) + α vel ​ MSE ​ ( Δ ​ x ^ , Δ ​ x ) . \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MoAE}}\;=\;\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{x},x)\;+\;\alpha_{\mathrm{vel}}\,\mathrm{MSE}(\Delta\hat{x},\Delta x). The velocity term is essential: without it, the MoAE collapses to emitting a per-sample mean pose at every frame, which would make z z insensitive to motion dynamics and defeat the diagnostic; the encoder must retain information about how the body moves, not only what poses it visits. Training: How2Sign train motions only, sequence length T = 200 T=200 frames, batch size 128 128 , 100 100 epochs, AdamW ( Loshchilov and Hutter, 2019 ) at lr 3 × 10 − 4 3\times 10^{-4} , dropout 0.1 0.1 (eval at dropout 0 0 ), bf16 mixed precision. The encoder is never exposed to model-generated motion during training, so the bottleneck does not learn collapse-specific features that could bias the diagnostic toward any particular generator. The same frozen ϕ \phi checkpoint is used to score every How2Sign diagnostic in this paper, removing per-paper FID-feature inconsistency. A separate MoAE of the same architecture is trained on Phoenix train motions only ( 7,096 7{,}096 sequences) and is used for the PT leak audit (Appendix C ). The MoAE-initialization and GT-vs-GT checks that validate the diagnostic are reported in Section 3.1 .

sections.heading: Cross-dataset ratios are qualitative, not quantitative.
sections.text: The two non-How2Sign diagnostics in this paper (gloss-level ASL3DWord, row 16 of Table 1 and Section 5.4 ; the PT leak audit on Phoenix-2014T, Appendix C ) use dataset-specific MoAEs trained on their own train splits, because the underlying motion representations differ (Phoenix: 2D MediaPipe keypoints; ASL3DWord: SMPL-X axis-angle FK-lifted to the same 44 × 3 44\times 3 upper-body 3D space as ϕ How2Sign \phi_{\text{How2Sign}} but on a 10 10 – 60 × 60\times smaller corpus). The ratios ρ div \rho_{\mathrm{div}} , ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} , ρ cond \rho_{\mathrm{cond}} are dimensionless within one ϕ \phi : numerator and denominator are L 2 distances in the same latent space, so the random-pairing baseline cancels the absolute scale. Therefore, within a single dataset, an ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} of 0.73 0.73 vs 0.96 0.96 means the model is genuinely more faithful, not that one ϕ \phi was “stricter”. Across datasets, however, the latent geometries differ and the same numerical ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} value need not correspond to identical motion quality. We use cross-dataset comparisons qualitatively only, to argue band membership (“ASL3DWord ρ faith = 0.73 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.73 matches that dataset’s own within-class ceiling of 0.752 0.752 , see Appendix A ; How2Sign ρ faith ∈ [ 0.89 , 1.00 ] \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}\in[0.89,1.00] collapses against a ceiling near 0 0 ”) rather than ordinal ranking of two distinct-dataset checkpoints by raw ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} .

sections.text: The diffusion ckpt’s ρ faith = 0.73 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.73 on the gloss-level ASL3DWord positive example (Section 5.4 , row 16 of Table 1 ) sits above the How2Sign-derived strict healthy threshold ρ faith < 0.7 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}<0.7 . To check whether the residual gap reflects real partial collapse or simply the MoAE’s own resolution limit on this dataset, we compute the within-ASL3DWord GT-vs-GT calibration: 339 339 test motions are encoded by the same ASL3DWord MoAE used elsewhere; pairwise L 2 distances in the latent are partitioned into same-gloss pairs ( 874 874 pairs, both encodings GT clips of the same target gloss) and different-gloss pairs ( 113,708 113{,}708 ). The same-gloss mean distance ( 0.826 0.826 ) divided by the different-gloss mean distance ( 1.098 1.098 ) gives ρ faith , ref = 0.752 \rho_{\mathrm{faith,ref}}=0.752 , the lowest ρ faith \rho_{\mathrm{faith}} achievable on this MoAE under perfect within-class generation, i.e. the metric’s intrinsic floor on ASL3DWord. The diffusion ckpt’s ρ faith = 0.73 \rho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.73 is 0.022 0.022 below this floor, meaning generated motion is, in the MoAE latent, on average as close to its target as a second GT clip of the same gloss. The residual gap from the How2Sign-derived 0.7 0.7 threshold is an MoAE timing- and encoder-noise floor inherent to ASL3DWord, not residual conditional collapse. Two practical consequences: (i) the ASL3DWord row of Table 1 is best interpreted as “healthy, at GT-pair parity” rather than “partially satisfied”; (ii) the gap between ASL3DWord ( 0.73 0.73 ) and the How2Sign collapse band ( [ 0.89 , 1.00 ] [0.89,1.00] ) understates the actual difference, because the How2Sign ceiling is near 0 0 (Section 3.1 ) whereas the ASL3DWord ceiling is 0.752 0.752 ; How2Sign checkpoints are ∼ 0.9 \sim 0.9 above their ceiling, ASL3DWord is at its ceiling.

sections.heading: Clean regression model.
sections.text: MotionRegressionModel is a 6 6 -layer Transformer decoder ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) with D = 512 D=512 , 8 8 heads, 0.1 0.1 dropout, GELU. The decoder’s queries are T T learnable positional embeddings; cross-attention memory is a single text token from frozen CLIP-ViT-B/32 ( Radford et al., 2021 ) . The output projects to 132 132 upper-body axis-angle dimensions. Training: AdamW ( β = ( 0.9 , 0.999 ) \beta=(0.9,0.999) , weight decay 10 − 2 10^{-2} ), OneCycleLR schedule with 5 % 5\% warmup and cosine annealing, fp16 mixed precision. Loss is ℒ pose + λ FK ​ ℒ FK \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pose}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{FK}}\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FK}} (per-frame pose MSE and FK joint-position MSE) with λ FK = 5 \lambda_{\mathrm{FK}}=5 . Total trainable parameters ∼ \sim 26 26 M (with frozen CLIP excluded).

sections.heading: Differences from Progressive Transformers (PT).
sections.text: The Clean regression model differs from PT ( Saunders et al., 2020 ) in four ways: (i) we generate all T T frames in a single forward pass, whereas PT is autoregressive (one frame at a time); (ii) output length T T is fixed per sample, whereas PT uses a learned step counter to decide when to stop — the source of PT’s inference-time leak (Appendix C ); (iii) the text encoder is frozen CLIP-ViT-B/32 (a single pooled token), whereas PT trains its own text encoder over T5-style tokenization; (iv) the decoder sees only the text embedding via cross-attention, with no feedback from previously generated frames. These simplifications remove PT’s inference-time leak surface and let the row report what a basic Transformer-decoder + + text cross-attention recipe achieves on How2Sign at the same paired-data budget.

sections.heading: Full prompt (verbatim).
sections.text: The prompt below is sent to the LLM once per sentence, with {input_sentence} replaced by the source text and the model’s next-token output read as the pseudo-gloss. The prompt is reproduced verbatim and spans multiple pages. You are an ASL (American Sign Language) linguistic expert. Your task is to extract pseudo-gloss from an English sentence. Pseudo-gloss is a sequence of words that determine the core meaning of the sentence. Each word should correspond to a distinct sign that an ASL signer would produce. The test is: "If I remove this word, does the core meaning of the sentence change?" Follow these three steps in order: ## Step 1: Phrase-level chunking Identify multi-word structures and treat them as a single unit BEFORE analyzing individual words: - Auxiliary verb chains: "is going to", "has been doing", "would have been", "are going to be learning" -> mark the entire chain as auxiliary, drop it all - Phrasal verbs: "get out", "pick up", "break down", "set up", "hold down" -> mark as a single verb unit, keep the particle - Light verb constructions: "make sure" -> "sure", "take a look" -> "look", "get rid of" -> "rid" -- the light verb (make/take/ get) is structural, drop it - Discourse frames: "let me/let’s" (when meaning "allow me to"), "you know", "I mean" -> drop This step is critical: without it, "going" inside "is going to" would be mistakenly kept as "go". ## Step 2: Decide which units determine the core meaning Keep words that would be produced as an independent sign in ASL: - Content words: nouns, verbs, adjectives, content adverbs (always, sometimes, often) - Pronouns: i, you, we, he, she, they, me, my, your, his, her, our, their - Negation: not, no, never, nothing, none, nobody - Interrogative WH-words: what, when, where, who, why, how, which (in questions) - Numbers: one, two, three, second, third, etc. - Modal verbs that carry meaning: can (ability), might/maybe (possibility), should/must (obligation) - Spatial/directional words when they express location or movement: inside, outside, up, down, around, forward, back, off, over Drop words that don’t change the core meaning: - Articles: a, an, the - Copulas: is, am, are, was, were (as linking verb) - Auxiliary chains identified in Step 1 - Conjunctions: and, but, or, so, because, if, that, then - Structural prepositions: of, to (infinitive marker), at, by, for, with, from (when purely grammatical) - Degree modifiers: very, really, pretty (as "fairly"), quite, extremely, a lot -- these are expressed through sign intensity in ASL, not as separate signs - Discourse fillers: okay, well, actually, basically, just, literally, essentially - Determiners: this, that, these, those, any, some (when not carrying meaning) - Relative pronouns: which/that introducing a clause ("the button, which opens..." -> drop "which") - Structural "how": "learn how to play" -> drop "how" (vs interrogative "How do you play?" -> keep "how") If the same content repeats for emphasis in the original sentence, keep it only once (de-duplicate). ## Step 3: Restore to citation form Lemmatize each kept word to its base/dictionary form: - Verb tense: gives->give, went->go, tied->tie, learning->learn, spoken->speak - Plural: steps->step, hands->hand, feet->foot, children->child - Comparative/superlative: highest->high, bigger->big, better->good - Never produce a non-word fragment (e.g. other->oth is WRONG, keep "other") ## Output format Output ONLY the pseudo-gloss as a single line of space-separated lowercase words. No explanation. ## Examples Sentence: Why? Gloss: why Sentence: I’m having fun. Gloss: i fun Sentence: The rudder is the vertical stabilizer. sections.heading: Appendix C Code-level audit of Progressive Transformers
sections.text: A prominent Phoenix SLP system, Progressive Transformers ( Saunders et al., 2020 ) , reports better BLEU than our checkpoints. Reading the released code, we find three inference/evaluation paths that leak ground-truth timing or length into the reported protocol; the two most important are (L1) the predicted counter scalar is overwritten by the GT counter at every decoder step, and (L2) the inference output length is set to the GT sequence length rather than learned via a stop signal.

sections.heading: Leaky-vs-fair experiment.
sections.text: We retrained PT’s released code on Phoenix-2014T at the paper’s native data scale and “best T2P” configuration, with no changes to architecture, loss, training, or inference logic, then ran inference twice on the same checkpoint over all 632 632 test sentences: once with leaks (L1)+(L2) intact (“leaky”), once with all three leaks off (“fair”, counter and length governed purely by the model’s predictions). Outputs were encoded with the Phoenix MoAE and d inter d_{\rm inter} / ρ div \rho_{\mathrm{div}} computed on the full test split (Table 4 ).

sections.heading: Representation and extraction.
sections.text: The independent PT retrainings in Section 2 use OpenPose-derived 3D joints ( Huang et al., 2021 ; Xie et al., 2024 ) or a SMPL-X representation ( Yin et al., 2024 ) , and PT’s original pipeline uses OpenPose. We instead extract Phoenix poses with MediaPipe Holistic, because OpenPose’s released codebase has very limited maintenance and is difficult to deploy in a modern environment. This extraction is imperfect: across the Phoenix train split, 28.6 % 28.6\% of left-hand and 23.9 % 23.9\% of right-hand frames are returned with no detection and are interpolated (see hand-detection notes below). We therefore use the leaky-vs-fair result only as a within-checkpoint comparison (the checkpoint, and any extraction artefact, is held fixed across the two inference passes, so the contrast still isolates the leak), and do not report absolute PT performance from our retraining; the OpenPose/SMPL-X retrainings in Section 2 are the appropriate reference for that. The checkpoint is held fixed, so the comparison isolates the leak’s effect. Metric Fair (no leak) Leaky (paper) d inter d_{\rm inter} 0.031 0.031 0.207 0.207 d inter ​ - ​ GT d_{\rm inter\text{-}GT} 2.321 2.321 2.321 2.321 ρ div \rho_{\mathrm{div}} (inter / GT) 0.013 0.089

sections.heading: Findings.
sections.text: (i) The leak measurably changes PT’s output. Toggling the GT-timing/length leak on the same trained checkpoint inflates the inter-sample spread d inter d_{\rm inter} from 0.031 0.031 to 0.207 0.207 and the diversity ratio ρ div \rho_{\mathrm{div}} from 0.013 0.013 to 0.089 0.089 , a roughly sevenfold change (Table 4 ). Because the checkpoint is held fixed across the two inference passes, this isolates the leak: the GT-aligned timing it supplies materially affects the generated motion and any statistic computed from it. (ii) Fair inference does not learn end-of-sequence in our text-to-pose setting. Without the GT counter, the predicted counter never crosses the stop threshold: every one of the 632 632 test samples runs to the 300 300 -frame cap, while GT lengths range from 3 3 to 89 89 frames. Under text conditioning, PT’s continuous-output decoder relies on (L1) for inference-time length supervision; a gloss-conditioned PT, whose input already encodes sign count, retains a partial length signal (leak-free gloss-to-pose PT reaches BLEU-4 4.04 4.04 ; Huang et al., 2021 ). The rest of this appendix gives the full L1–L3 enumeration, the training setup for the leaky-vs-fair experiment, and the supporting pose-extractor, hand-detection, and bug-fix notes needed to make the released code execute under modern tooling.

sections.heading: Three inference- and evaluation-time leaks.
sections.text: Inspection of the released repository identifies the following three paths through which GT timing or length information enters PT’s reported numerical protocol: (L1) search.py :55–63: at every decoder step the predicted counter scalar c ^ t \hat{c}_{t} is overwritten with the GT counter c t ∗ c^{*}_{t} before being fed back. The author comment in the file reads: “ Drive the timing by giving the GT timing ”. (L2) search.py :46: the inference output length is assigned from the GT target length rather than learned via a stop signal. (L3) Configs/Base.yaml :25,29: the only validation/early-stopping metric is the DTW score itself, so the reported quantitative results come from this GT-aligned distance.

sections.heading: Training setup and toggle list.
sections.text: Training matched the paper’s data scale ( ∼ \sim 7 000 7\,000 training sequences) and the published “best T2P” configuration ( 2 2 encoder/decoder layers, 4 4 heads, 512 512 embedding dim, MSE loss, future-prediction FP = 10 \mathrm{FP}{=}10 , Gaussian-noise augmentation rate 5 5 ). Training reached lr min \mathrm{lr}_{\min} at step 1450 1450 , with best validation DTW = 15.76 =15.76 at step 450 450 . The “leaky” inference configuration in Table 4 leaves (L1)+(L2) intact (matching the paper’s reported protocol up to BLEU back-translation); the “fair” configuration disables all three leaks listed above (counter is purely autoregressive, output length is governed by a predicted-counter stop rule capped at the global 300 300 -frame limit, and the DTW-aligned distance is no longer used as the model-selection metric). Both inference passes were run over all 632 632 test sentences on the same trained checkpoint.

sections.heading: Pose extraction divergence from the original paper.
sections.text: Saunders et al. ( Saunders et al., 2020 ) use OpenPose followed by 2D-to-3D inverse-kinematics lifting; we substitute MediaPipe Holistic upper-body keypoints because the OpenPose pipeline is impractical to re-deploy on contemporary GPU toolchains and the extraction is not released. The two extractors differ in keypoint set and 2D-vs-3D representation, but the total paired-sample budget is identical at ∼ \sim 7 000 7\,000 training sequences, so the leak audit still applies; what we cannot precisely reproduce are the absolute pose-space FID values (which depend on extraction).

sections.heading: Hand-detection failure rate.
sections.text: MediaPipe Holistic produces all-zero hand keypoints when detection confidence is below threshold. Across the Phoenix train split, the mean per-video fraction of fully-missing left-hand frames is 28.6 % 28.6\% (max 100 % 100\% ); for the right hand 23.9 % 23.9\% (max 84 % 84\% ). We linearly-interpolate within each clip and fall back to the corresponding body wrist when an entire hand is missing throughout, so PT does not train against zero-hand targets.

sections.heading:
Bug fixes required to run the released code under a
modern deep-learning toolchain.
sections.text: We applied six small patches to make the released code execute under the current toolchain. None of the patches touch the architecture, loss, training loop, validation loss/DTW computation, model selection, or inference/search code : the model and training-relevant files ( model.py , transformer_layers.py , encoders.py , decoders.py , embeddings.py , loss.py , search.py , data.py , batch.py , vocabulary.py ) are byte-for-byte the released versions. The patches are: removing the deprecated verbose kwarg from ReduceLROnPlateau ( builders.py:137 ); fixing an undefined train_output reference ( prediction.py:73 ); removing a redundant FP-cut on the inference output already cut in search.py:greedy ( prediction.py:74 ); making plot_videos.py:47 adaptive to MediaPipe’s 67 67 -joint layout; wrapping produce_validation_video in try/except to swallow bone-graph mismatches at validation-video render time (the _save_checkpoint call lies outside the try block, so model selection is unaffected); and adding weights_only=False to torch.load ( helpers.py:202 ). Total diff vs the upstream repo: 32 32 lines added, 20 20 lines removed across 5 5 files.

sections.heading: Reproducibility.
sections.text: The patched code, training and audit scripts, configurations, and all per-sample inference outputs are available alongside the paper. Reproducing Table 4 end-to-end requires only a single GPU.

sections.heading: Training setup.
sections.text: Our back-translation (motion-to-text) evaluator on How2Sign is trained pose-to-text with translation cross-entropy only, no gloss-CTC loss, no pretrained CSLR features, no auxiliary pretraining. Input is axis-angle SMPL-X; decoding at evaluation is beam- 5 5 ; the test split has n = 2,357 n=2{,}357 paired sentences. In this regime BT-BLEU-4 plateaus at a ceiling of ≈ 2.5 \approx 2.5 even on GT motion, and cross-regime comparisons against gloss-CTC-supervised evaluators (e.g. Sign Language Transformers ( Camgoz et al., 2020 ) ) are not directly meaningful.

sections.heading: Failure-mode commentary on the examples.
sections.text: Section 5.3 (Table 2 ) shows 3 3 representative GT/prediction pairs at our BLEU-4 = 1.24 =1.24 checkpoint, in the same regime as the BLEU-4 ≈ 1.22 \approx 1.22 no-pretraining baseline of Uthus et al. (2023) . The pattern is consistent across the test split: (i) input-independent high-frequency template language — instructional constructions (“you can do it”, “you want to make sure”, “i’m going to take my right/left hand”) and pronoun-heavy filler — whose semantic content is unrelated to the GT motion; and (ii) degenerate end-of-sequence repetition (“very light, very light, very light, … \ldots ”). Both patterns are characteristic of an autoregressive decoder estimating a near-marginal language-model prior with negligible conditional signal from the encoded motion.

Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2606.01643v1 [cs.CV] 01 Jun 2026 Conditional Collapse in Sign Language Production: A Diagnostic and a Scaling Argument Rui Hong Affiliation: George Mason University Email: rhong5@gmu.edu Jana Košecká Affiliation: George Mason University Email: kosecka@gmu.edu Abstract Sign Language Production (SLP) is the task of generating avatar sign language motion from natural language text. The quality of the generated motion is typically evaluated by a motion-space Fréchet distance (FID) and back-translation (BT) BLEU score on benchmarks such as How2Sign. Both metrics can improve substantially while the underlying generator fails to faithfully represent the sign language gestures. In this work we propose to evaluate the generated motion at three independent levels: ( τ 1 	au_{1} ) initial-pose conditioning, ( τ 2 	au_{2} ) output diversity, and ( τ 3 	au_{3} ) target faithfulness. We compute these as pairwise-distance ratios using latent representations of a frozen motion autoencoder (MoAE). We evaluate 14 14 SLP model checkpoints on How2Sign dataset ( Duarte et al., 2021 ) , including a re-implemented Neural Sign Actors (NSA) ( Baltatzis et al., 2024 ) , and show that τ 3 	au_{3} faithfulness is never attained, while FID varies by nearly two orders of magnitude and is uncorrelated with faithfulness. We show that on the isolated gloss dataset ASL3DWord ( Dong et al., 2024a ) favorable τ 3 	au_{3} can be attained, hence isolating the size of the sentence-level paired-dataset as the bottleneck. 1 Introduction Text-to-motion systems report steady improvements on standard quantitative benchmarks. Reliable evaluation of text-to-motion generation requires metrics that respond to whether each output is faithful to its specific input, not merely to whether outputs look like plausible samples from the training distribution. We study this requirement in sentence-level Sign Language Production (SLP), where recent systems on How2Sign ( Duarte et al., 2021 ) report steadily improving Fréchet distance (FID), computed over motion features, and back-translation (BT) BLEU score, and declare progress toward usable text-to-sign generation. We argue that both headline metrics can rise while the underlying generator remains essentially text-independent. FID rewards an anatomically valid mean motion that ignores the input over a model that follows the input but produces slightly noisier motion. It can thus prefer a collapsed generator over a faithful one, as we observe on How2Sign (§ 5.2 ); back-translation BLEU is bounded by a BT model that itself collapses to high-frequency boilerplate, so it reflects token-frequency overlap rather than motion-text correspondence. In this work, we propose novel evaluation and diagnostic metrics that reveal conditional collapse in Sign Language Production on state-of-the-art datasets. Contributions. (i) Given any text-to-motion model and a held-out test set, we encode both ground-truth motions and model generations through a frozen motion autoencoder MoAE (a small transformer) trained once on the target dataset’s ground-truth motions, compressing each motion into a compact latent vector and reconstructing it. We then compute three pairwise-distance ratios in that space, varying the sentence conditioning and comparing the generated and ground-truth motions. (ii) We identify three indicators of conditional collapse at different levels: an initial-pose level ( τ 1 	au_{1} ), an output diversity level ( τ 2 	au_{2} ), and a faithfulness level ( τ 3 	au_{3} ) that can be attained independently , with visual and quantitative evidence (§ 4 ). (iii) We transfer the same generative diffusion model backbone to the gloss-level ASL3DWord benchmark, showing that it attains significantly better τ 3 	au_{3} , suggesting that sentence-level paired-data scale is a major bottleneck for How2Sign within the architecture space we tested (§ 5.4 , Figure 3 ). The failures we document are diagnosable and motivate three concrete changes. The field should (a) report the diagnostic ratios alongside FID and back-translation BLEU; (b) be transparent about the paired-data budget and any auxiliary pretraining corpora; and (c) treat the faithfulness level ( τ 3 	au_{3} ) as an important criterion when designing future models (§ 6 ). 2 Related Work Sign Language Production. Sentence-level SLP approaches fall into two families. Regression-based approaches formulate the problem as sequence to (continuous) pose sequence translation and predict a deterministic pose stream: Progressive Transformers (PT) ( Saunders et al., 2020 ) use an autoregressive transformer with a learned step-counter scalar over a T5-style text encoder; Huang et al. (2021) replace the autoregressive decoder with a non-autoregressive parallel decoder, an external aligner for gloss-duration prediction, and a spatial-temporal graph-convolutional pose generator on Phoenix-2014T; T2S-GPT ( Yin et al., 2024 ) encodes Phoenix-2014T SMPL-X poses with a dynamic-length VQ-VAE and autoregressively generates pose codes from text with a GPT-style decoder. Diffusion-based approaches train a generative model of human motion conditioned on text describing human action sequences. For example MDM ( Tevet et al., 2023 ) is a transformer denoising model conditioned on text describing general sequences of actions encoded with a frozen CLIP encoder; G2P-DDM ( Xie et al., 2024 ) encodes Phoenix-2014T poses with a VQ-VAE and runs discrete denoising diffusion in the discrete latent space; Neural Sign Actors ( Baltatzis et al., 2024 ) uses a GNN + LSTM denoising model on SMPL-X parameters. Hong and Kosecka (2026) build a MDM-style backbone at the gloss level on ASL3DWord ( Dong et al., 2024a ) (a WLASL ( Li et al., 2020 ) subset; 1.2 1.2 K clips, 103 103 glosses) and report usable generation; we apply the same backbone to sentence-level How2Sign and find that gloss-scale conclusions do not transfer. Sign Language Translation (SLT) SLP approaches are often evaluated by back-translating generated human motions to text using a learned sign-to-text model, and reporting BLEU score. Three SLT families recur: the joint CSLR + + SLT Sign Language Transformers ( Camgoz et al., 2020 ) , which couples a gloss-CTC loss with translation; plain encoder–decoders over pretrained video features (e.g. Tarrés et al. (2023) , Kinetics-I3D, no gloss-CTC); and discrete-token translation pretrained on large corpora (YouTube-ASL ( Uthus et al., 2023 ) , 11 11 K hours). The two recurring datasets differ in vocabulary, reporting low BLEU-4 score for non-pretrained BT models: weather-domain Phoenix-2014T ( Forster et al., 2014 ) has ∼ \sim 1,066 1{,}066 German (DGS) gloss types in ∼ \sim 7 7 K sentence-motion pairs, whereas on open-domain How2Sign ( Duarte et al., 2021 ) ( ∼ \sim 15 15 K words, ∼ \sim 31 31 K pairs) the highest attained BLEU-4 score is far lower. In the no-pretraining regime Uthus et al. (2023) report How2Sign BLEU-4 ≈ 1.22 \approx 1.22 and our own BT model plateaus at a BLEU-4 ceiling of ≈ 2.5 \approx 2.5 even on GT motion; Tarrés et al. (2023) reach 8.03 8.03 via I3D pretraining and Uthus et al. (2023) ≈ 12 \approx 12 via pre-training on 11 11 K hours of videos from YouTubeASL dataset. By contrast, Saunders et al. (2020) and Baltatzis et al. (2024) report BLEU-4 of 10.51 10.51 and 13.12 13.12 without describing auxiliary pretraining, the latter exceeding both the pretrained YouTube-ASL number and our GT-motion BLEU-4 score. Independent re-trainings of Progressive Transformers (PT) in the three SLP papers above place BLEU-4 well below these numbers. Huang et al. (2021) retrain PT on OpenPose 3D joints (gloss-to-pose, no GT timing at inference) and report BLEU-4 1.59 1.59 for the base model and 4.04 4.04 for the future-prediction/Gaussian-noise variant. Xie et al. (2024) report 4.04 4.04 BLEU-4 and note that PT’s original numbers depend on ground-truth first-frame and timing information. Yin et al. (2024) retrain PT on a SMPL-X 6 6 D-rotation representation (text-to-pose) and report BLEU-4 of 4.38 4.38 . Across two input representations and both task settings, independently retrained PTs fall in the 1.6 1.6 – 4.4 4.4 range. FID critiques. The limitations of Frechet Distance (FID) for conditional generation are well known in the text-to-image ( Kynkäänniemi et al., 2023 ) and text-to-motion ( Guo et al., 2022 ) literatures, and alternatives such as paired R-precision, MM-Distance and MultiModality have been proposed. Our diagnostic is in this spirit but specifically targets the conditional-mean collapse blindness dominant in SLP. Pose-based SL generation evaluation. Most directly adjacent, Jiang et al. (2025) meta-evaluate existing pose-based sign language metrics by correlation with human judgements and rank them by quality. Beyond the mean-motion mechanism of § 3 , a model whose outputs match the GT distribution but are paired with the wrong inputs also gets a low FID; neither case matches what a reader expects from a small FID number. The blind spot is worse in SLP because GT motion varies in a small range anatomical envelope) and test sets are typically only a few hundred motions. Reproducibility note on Neural Sign Actors. Neural Sign Actors ( Baltatzis et al., 2024 ) reports the lowest sentence-level How2Sign FID in the literature but releases neither code nor weights. Following the published description, our re-implementation needed several debugging rounds (gradient-norm clipping, loss-formulation fixes) to converge, and even then our best run reaches FID ≈ 151 \approx 151 (an order of magnitude above the reported value), with ρ faith ≈ 1.00 ho_{\mathrm{faith}}\approx 1.00 and no input-specific motion in rendered samples. We do not interpret this discrepancy, and it does not affect our claim: at the How2Sign 26K budget even an NSA-class FID is consistent with τ 1 	au_{1} / τ 2 	au_{2} satisfied + + τ 3 	au_{3} collapsed, the regime our 14 14 How2Sign checkpoints occupy. We read prior FID gains in this line as improvements in τ 1 	au_{1} and partial τ 2 	au_{2} , not τ 3 	au_{3} . Recommended evaluation protocol. We recommend SLP papers report all three ratios alongside FID: ρ faith ho_{\mathrm{faith}} as a bright-line check (treat ρ faith ≥ 0.95 ho_{\mathrm{faith}}\geq 0.95 as failure), and ρ div ho_{\mathrm{div}} to separate “random anatomical poses” (low ρ div ho_{\mathrm{div}} ) from “diverse but mis-aligned outputs” (near-GT ρ div ho_{\mathrm{div}} ). Computing the diagnostic on a shared external motion MoAE (we release ours, Appendix A ) also removes the per-paper-MoAE inconsistency behind FID drift across the literature. The diagnostic is parameter-free and adds negligible cost on top of standard generation. Bidirectional evidence of the data bottleneck. The bottleneck is independently visible in the sign-to-text direction. Uthus et al. (2023) report that a translator trained directly on How2Sign reaches only BLEU-4 ≈ 1.22 \approx 1.22 , consistent with output dominated by high-frequency boilerplate (§ 5.3 , Table 2 ), with faithful translation emerging only after 11 11 K hours of pretraining. Our text-to-motion experiments reach the symmetric conclusion: ρ faith ho_{\mathrm{faith}} never leaves the collapse band on How2Sign 26K and the 13 13 K → 	o 26 26 K gradient does not improve it. The bottleneck is the same in both directions: How2Sign’s 26 26 K paired sentences are below what is needed to learn the motion–text correspondence. What would satisfy τ 3 	au_{3} ? The most concrete candidate is large-scale text-to-motion pretraining on an auxiliary corpus: the YouTube-ASL translator becomes faithful in the sign-to-text direction only after 11 11 K hours of pretraining, and a similarly-scaled motion pretrain may transfer to text-to-motion. 7 Conclusion We introduced a diagnostic that exposes conditional collapse in sentence-level Sign Language Production, and used it to establish that the How2Sign paired-data scale is a major bottleneck on the faithfulness level ( τ 3 	au_{3} ) within the architecture space we tested, with collapse persisting across data quantity and input unit length. A best-effort reimplementation of Neural Sign Actors places it in the same τ 3 	au_{3} -collapsed regime as the rest of our checkpoints, while the same diffusion backbone and loss transferred unchanged to gloss-level ASL3DWord satisfies τ 3 	au_{3} ( ρ faith = 0.73 ho_{\mathrm{faith}}=0.73 ), consistent with sentence-level paired-data scale being a major bottleneck within the architecture space we tested. The FID–alignment disconnect we document argues for a field-wide protocol change: SLP papers should report ( ρ cond , ρ div , ρ faith ) (ho_{\mathrm{cond}},ho_{\mathrm{div}},ho_{\mathrm{faith}}) alongside FID and BLEU, and treat ρ faith ≥ 0.95 ho_{\mathrm{faith}}\geq 0.95 as a clear failure.
